chunks: How a charge pump raises voltage. The question: How does a charge pump boost voltage?
A charge pump raises the voltage by stacking a charged capacitor on top of the input, like two batteries in series. First the capacitor charges to V in .
Then its bottom plate (one of its two metal sides) is moved up to V in , so its top plate sits at 2 volts in .
Power is conserved, so the input current is about twice the output current. To get bigger multiples, you chain more stages.
Think of two batteries. One alone gives 3 volts. Stack them end to end and you get 6 volts at the ends.
The charge pump creates that second "battery" by charging a capacitor, then connecting it in series with the supply.
A capacitor's voltage cannot jump instantly, so when its bottom plate is lifted, its top plate rises along with it.
Unlike a real battery, the capacitor must be recharged every cycle.
Phase 1: the capacitor charges to V in (plus on top). The output capacitor holds the output.
Flying capacitor: the capacitor that gets charged, then stacked on the input ("How a charge pump works").
Series stacking: connecting voltage sources end to end so their voltages add. Charge: the amount of electricity moved, which is current times time.
Stage: one capacitor-and-switch (or diode) section of a multi-stage pump. Dickson pump: a chain of diodes and capacitors in which each stage adds roughly one more input voltage.
Take a 3 volts input and a doubler. Phase one: the capacitor charges to 3 volts. Phase two: its bottom is at 3 volts, so its top is at 6 volts and feeds the output.
Say the load draws 10 milliamps at 6 volts, which is 60 milliwatts. The input supplies 3 volts at 20 milliamps, which is also 60 milliwatts.
Voltage doubled, current halved, power the same (ideally). That is the whole idea.
"It's series stacking. Charge a capacitor to V in , then in the next phase put its bottom plate on V in , so its top plate is at 2 volts in , and connect that to the output.
Energy is conserved because the input supplies charge twice per cycle but the output only gets it once: input current is twice output current.
More stages stack more clock swings, about (N plus 1)V in , at the price of more droop and diode drops."
Quick check. Why does the output of a doubler reach about 2 volts in ?
